content: The early introduction of complementary feeding (CF) before 4 months of age, compared to initiation at or after 4 months, has been evaluated in various studies. These studies have examined outcomes such as body mass index (BMI), overweight and obesity, lower respiratory tract infections (LRTI), and other health parameters. The findings are summarized below: 1. BMI and Overweight/Obesity: Early introduction of CF (<4 months) was associated with a higher BMI in some studies. For overweight and obesity, the incidence was reported as 216 per 1,000 infants, with 24 fewer cases per 1,000 (ranging from 140 fewer to 187 more cases) when CF was introduced later. 2. Lower Respiratory Tract Infections (LRTI): The incidence of LRTI was 139 per 1,000 infants, with 28 fewer cases per 1,000 (ranging from 70 fewer to 36 more cases) when CF was introduced later. 3. Risk of Bias in Studies: Many studies had unclear or moderate risks of bias due to issues such as blinding, attrition, and timing of exposure assessment. Some studies were downgraded by one or two levels in quality due to high heterogeneity, small sample sizes, or fewer than 300 events. 4. Health Outcomes in Preterm or Low Birth Weight Infants: For preterm or low birth weight infants, early CF introduction at 4 months compared to 6 months showed mixed results. Severe anemia (hemoglobin <100 g/L) and other health outcomes were evaluated, but the evidence was limited by small sample sizes and high risks of bias. 5. Thinning and Weight: Early CF introduction (<6 months) compared to ≥6 months showed a higher incidence of thinness (151 per 1,000, with 65 more cases per 1,000) and weight-related outcomes (114 per 1,000, with 17 more cases per 1,000). 6. Obesity and Atopic Dermatitis: The incidence of obesity was 51 per 1,000, with 18 fewer cases per 1,000 (ranging from 40 fewer to 45 more cases) when CF was introduced later. For atopic dermatitis, the incidence was 180 per 1,000, with 17 more cases per 1,000 (ranging from 17 fewer to 58 more cases). 7. Food Allergy: Early CF introduction (<6 months) was associated with a higher incidence of food allergies (21 per 1,000, with 43 more cases per 1,000, ranging from 13 fewer to 331 more cases). 8. Study Limitations: Many studies were not adjusted for confounding factors, and heterogeneity was common. Confidence intervals were often broad, and the number of participants or events was frequently below the threshold for robust conclusions. 9. References and Evidence Base: The findings are based on systematic reviews and randomized controlled trials, including those published in reputable journals such as The Lancet, American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, and Pediatrics. These studies evaluated the timing of CF introduction and its impact on growth, nutritional status, and health outcomes in infants. In conclusion, the timing of complementary feeding introduction has significant implications for infant health, but the evidence is often limited by methodological issues and variability in study designs. Further high-quality research is needed to provide clearer guidance.
